people don't quite seem to be noticing, but we're entering an era where almost everything can be imbued with small sparks of intelligence. models aren't yet human-expert level at pushing the frontier of LLM development, but they *do* seem to be ~near superhuman at classical ML research. you can just *make neural networks that do things* these days, at levels of accuracy and ambition that would have been impossible even three years ago. apple and tesla releasing depth pro and third person view simultaneously are signs of this, but it's everywhere. people are making mini neural nets for webpages that syntax highlight arbitrary text or predict layouts to avoid pop-in. grainy webcams are getting hyper-accurate pose estimation. incredible speech to text and text to speech open source models that can run on a fuckin raspberry pi CPU or smart watch. if you're a gamedev and ask a frontier model, you can just get your own version of DLSS hyper-turned for your own game, and *for cheap*. your wifi network is a room scale presence detector, and you can just get a mini model turned on personal specifics of your space. it's all there at everyone's fingertips.

for so long neural networks, computer vision, etc have required expertise, been expensive and tough to wrangle, and especially recently cheap LLMs have just obviously been the way to go instead. but when you have a horde of experts happy to poke at individual weights, you can unlock things that just weren't even possible before.

all forms of computer hardware are no longer depreciating assets. stop throwing them away, selling them, trading them in. every one will only exponentially increase in utility from here on out.

posts.text:
Happy Thanksgiving, Americans:

It's a lovely holiday, and it's in keeping with the essentially generous spirit of you Yankees. It's one thing to be wealthy, as you are, but it's another to be generous in your thanks for the opportunities that you have been provided with. Hard work and intelligence make people rich, at least in truly productive and honest societies, but that hard work and intelligence can be in part what is provided to you by your culture and those whose supreme efforts gave rise to it.

Remembering that is salutary.

One of the most costly psychological errors—terrible in its consequences, both individually and socially—is resentment. It is, I suppose, a form of envy—I don't have what he has been granted—and it poisons individuals and societies alike. Gratitude is the antidote to resentment, and should well be cultured, as it is in the US, for precisely that reason.

I have had more opportunity than usual in the last year to consider the relationship between the two. I'm still very ill, and it is generally very painful. Under such conditions, resentment comes all too easily, and does nothing but add a toxicity of conception and emotion to an already difficult situation. But how to avoid it?

Conscious practice of gratitude.

I have a wife and children and friends and other family whose loyalty has gone above and beyond what is merely admirable to the near miraculous. I have a support and security team about whom the same can be said. I have been able to work some again—both writing something new and working on Peterson Academy late at night. Under the circumstances, both are going well.

I can't say I always manage it, but it is good and right for me to be thankful about all that, even when the pain is overwhelming—and a holiday that makes a celebration out of gratitude provides the opportunity to reflect upon the advantages that I still retain.

Count your blessings—and happy Thanksgiving.

I'm Sam, one of Anthropic's co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I'm going to have more to share on that work over the coming months.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.

Trump's intervention to rescue Nvidia may have revived the stock market, but economist Jeffrey Currie argues it did absolutely nothing to address the underlying credit crisis threatening America's AI boom.

Unlike the incredibly profitable software business model of the past, today's tech giants are spending enormous amounts of borrowed money building physical infrastructure.

Some are spending more cash than they generate, while simultaneously draining capital, labour and raw materials from the rest of the economy.

And now the Federal Reserve faces a potentially devastating dilemma.

Keep interest rates high and risk collapsing the AI bubble that is sustaining U.S economic growth, or cut rates while the Iran war threatens to send oil prices soaring.

Jeffrey believes the Fed will ultimately be forced to cut rates, ushering in an era of higher inflation and currency debasement.

He's already exited his tech investments and returned to oil, while watching for a Fed pivot that could trigger a dramatic rally in gold.

He also sees striking parallels with the 2014 shale bubble, when investors were obsessed with oil companies and wanted nothing to do with tech stocks.

Today, those roles have completely reversed.

If he's right, we could be approaching one of the greatest rotations of wealth from technology into hard assets in modern history.
